content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper argues that the need of long inference steps in DDPM is due to the bias of inference network output and the ground -truth from the forward process. The paper proposes DDPM-IP by adding a Gaussian noise to the intermediate output of the revsersed diffusion process, hoping to reduce the error in each step of the generation process and reduce the inference steps. Experiments show that this method gives better FID results on Cifar10 and ImageNet using 125 steps than the baseline method using 1000 steps.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. Empirically, DDPM-IP is demonstrated to improve the image quality and significantly reduce the sampling steps during inference.
2 DDPM-IP is straightforward and does not require any changes to the network structure or to the specific loss function. This simplicity makes it easy to be replicated and inserted into existing DDPMs.
3 There are no domain-specific assumptions in this method, so it can be applied more generally to other domains.

Weaknesses:
1. There seems to be fundamental flaw in the proposed method. Basically, the authors assume that the bias between the model's input x^t and the ground-truth xt from the forward process is Gaussian distributed. It is not clear why this is the case (in fact, I don't believe the bias is a simple zero-mean Gaussian). To verify this is indeed a reasonable approximation, the authors at least need to show that with the addition of this Gaussian noise, the prediction from the model at training are closer to the true from the forward process. Unfortunately, the authors only show the bias in the standard ADM model (e.g., in Table 1), there is no evidence showing the bias can be mitigated after adding in the noise.

In fact, if one look at eq.7, adding in the noise can be considered as using a different noise schedule in the forward process, which is essentially the same as the standard DDPM. So I think the empirical improvement merely comes from tuning the noise schedule in the forward process, instead of the claimed input bias problem.

Also, the authors add the same noise to the real case of xt at all times, however the real situation may be that the difference between xt and x^t is actually different at different times. The authors need to justify the addition of the same noise for different time step..

2. It is claimed that the proposed method can achieve higher FID results at 125 sampling steps than the original method at 1000 steps, however, the authors also mention that the image generation results are better at 100-300 sampling steps than at 1000 steps, so it is unfair to compare 125 steps with 1000 steps and make this claim.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity
The presentation and writing are clear. The proposed method is simple,

Quality:
The proposed method is plausible. The demonstration of the claim is not well supported. And the experimental design and empirical evidence are inadequate.

Novelty:
The problem of generative-inference gap in diffusion models is novel, but the solution to this problem is not satisfactory.

Reproductivity:
The authors have not yet released the source code, so it is difficult to judge whether it can be reproduced.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposes the problem of generative-inference gap in diffusion generative models. However, the proposed solution is problematic and not well justified, and I don't think it can solve this problem.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.

content.title: Response to Reviewer Cr6u
content.comment:
Thank you very much for the reviews and insightful comments. We are sorry for our late response due to the stretched GPU resources and heavy experiments.

> There seems to be fundamental flaw in the proposed method. Basically, the authors assume that the bias between the model's input x^t and the ground-truth xt from the forward process is Gaussian distributed. It is not clear why this is the case (in fact, I don't believe the bias is a simple zero-mean Gaussian). To verify this is indeed a reasonable approximation, the authors at least need to show that with the addition of this Gaussian noise, the prediction from the model at training are closer to the true from the forward process. Unfortunately, the authors only show the bias in the standard ADM model (e.g., in Table 1), there is no evidence showing the bias can be mitigated after adding in the noise.

We empirically show that the prediction errors between the predicted x_t and ground truth x_t at different $t$ are Gaussian distributed with zero means. The reason for this is that the model is trained to be as close to the ground truth x_t as possible during training.

Input perturbation does achieve a lower exposure bias in our experiments and we will add the results and further discussions in the future version. 


> In fact, if one look at eq.7, adding in the noise can be considered as using a different noise schedule in the forward process, which is essentially the same as the standard DDPM. So I think the empirical improvement merely comes from tuning the noise schedule in the forward process, instead of the claimed input bias problem.

Yes, the combination of the two independent Gaussians ($\epsilon + \gamma \xi $) is another Gaussian. But the key to input perturbation is the asymmetry between the input signal and the supervision signal. The experiments on Cifar10 below demonstrate that the improvement comes from the input perturbation, rather than a new noise schedule ($\epsilon + \gamma \xi $) in the forward diffusion.

| **model**     | **input signal**         | **supversion signal**    | **best FID** |
|---------------|--------------------------|--------------------------|--------------|
| ADM           | $\epsilon$               | $\epsilon$               | 3.56         |
| new noise ADM | $\epsilon + \gamma \xi $ | $\epsilon + \gamma \xi $ | 4.09         |
| ADM-IP        | $\epsilon + \gamma \xi $ | $\epsilon$               | 3.12         |)


> Also, the authors add the same noise to the real case of xt at all times, however the real situation may be that the difference between xt and x^t is actually different at different times. The authors need to justify the addition of the same noise for different time step..

We use the same $\gamma _{t}$ over all timesteps for two reasons. One is that searching for the optimal $\gamma _{t}$ for each timestep is expensive, and another reason is that the model is easier to train under the same $\gamma _{t}$. It is likely that the same $\gamma _{t}$ strategy is sub-optimal, we would like to put it in our future work.


> It is claimed that the proposed method can achieve higher FID results at 125 sampling steps than the original method at 1000 steps, however, the authors also mention that the image generation results are better at 100-300 sampling steps than at 1000 steps, so it is unfair to compare 125 steps with 1000 steps and make this claim.

Thanks for the suggestion, we would modify the comparison in our subsequent paper modification.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper points out the prediction error that existed in the current diffusion models, specifically the denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM), which could be potentially accumulated as the denoising steps go up. As a solution, the authors propose adding additional noise perturbation reweighted with a timestep-related hyperparameter at each timestep in training. The authors further show connections with Lipschitz constrain and their empirical results that this input perturbation could further improve the sampling efficiency.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**

The paper is well-written and organized, making it easy to follow. The proposed solution is simple, without further requirements to modify the model or training scheme. The authors also make connections to previous studies of making Lipschitz constrain in generative modeling. From the empirical perspective, the authors have shown their main experiments reasonably, and the details are included for reproducibility. 

**Weakness**

Although the proposed method is simple, it introduces a new hyper-parameter $\gamma_t$ that controls the weight of input perturbation. The authors do not include experiments regarding how this hyper-parameter affects the model. 

As the authors point out, there exists a gap between training and sampling, it would be great if the authors can quantify this gap and show some relation between this gap and the choice of $\gamma_t$. Also, the choice of $\gamma_t$ matters when making connection to gradient penalty and weight decay. 

The authors may need to show whether the proposed input perturbation is complementary or replicated with gradient penalty and weight decay, otherwise, this may weaken the contribution of this method. 

As a plug-in method to diffusion model and recently there are various choices in speeding up the sampling, e.g., DDIM, the authors may need to explore if input perturbation can be compatible with these techniques.

The baseline experiment settings are changed in the comparison. For example, the baseline model used in the paper (ADM) conducts experiments on ImageNet 64x64 and LSUN 256x256. The FID evolution shown in Fig. 2 (a), (b) does not seem to be converged. 

**Some typos / other minors**

Section 1.  

Paragraph1-Line 4: differently -> Different

Paragraph2-Line 9: $\mu(\hat x_t, t)$ -> $\mu(\hat x_{t+1}, t)$

Section 4.

Paragraph2-Line 8: citation format. 

Paragraph3-Line 1: $\bar \sigma_t$ is not defined in the text.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity and Quality**

The paper is overall clear to the readers. I list some points that are not precise below:

The illustration of Figure 1 can be ambiguous and misleading. Although the green trajectory is shorter than the red one, the starting points of these two lines are not the same. If the authors would like to show that the proposed method can correct the prediction error in the intermediate steps, it is clearer to let these two tractories have the same starting point and compare them. 

In Algorithm3, which is proposed to measure the prediction error in the inference stage, each time $x_t$ is constructed with the forward function given ground-truth $x_0$. However, as the authors emphasize in the paper, in the inference, the reverse process often starts from $x_T$ and $x_0$ is not seen. The results shown in Table 1 are more like the reconstruction error of ADM, but does it measure the discrepancy between training and inference? 

For the experiments, the authors apply ADM as the backbone trained with 1000 steps and sampled with different steps. The notation of both training and sampling steps are duplicated and might be more precise with different notations. 

For sampling T=1000, the authors need to clarify whether they use the sampling strategy in Algorithm 2 or 3, i.e., whether they omit $\sigma_t z$. 

**Novelty**

The proposed method has novelty in improving the DDPM forward function, while it has the same effects with gradient penalty (GP) and weight decay (WD), which might have been used in some implementations as technical tricks but not discussed in the paper. A more comprehensive study might be needed as it is not clear whether the proposed IP method is orthogonal or complementary to GP and WD. In such a context, the authors may need to show the uniqueness compared with GP and WD to enhance the novelty.


**Reproducibility**

The authors include details for the algorithm and model parameterization, which should be useful for reproducing their results.
content.summary_of_the_review: The problem pointed out in this paper is important in the study of diffusion model. The proposed method is also simple and shows improvements compared with baselines. However, some key perspectives regarding the proposed method are not comprehensively studied and thus remain unclear to the readers. I would mark this paper below the acceptance borderline and look forward to the authors' responses.

content.title: Response to Reviewer e8hz
content.comment:
Thank you very much for the comments. We are sorry for our late response due to the stretched GPU resources and heavy experiments.

 > Although the proposed method is simple, it introduces a new hyper-parameter $\gamma_{t}$ that controls the weight of input perturbation. The authors do not include experiments regarding how this hyper-parameter affects the model.

We actually searched for $\gamma_{t}$ from 0 to 0.3 and set $\gamma_{t} = 0.1$ for its best performance. One can treat input perturbation as a specific regularization regarding the choice of $\gamma_{t}$, therefore, small $\gamma_{t}$ would have little effect on the smoothness of the prediction function, large $\gamma_{t}$ would over-smooth the neural network. 

> As the authors point out, there exists a gap between training and sampling, it would be great if the authors can quantify this gap and show some relation between this gap and the choice of $\gamma_{t}$. Also, the choice of $\gamma_{t}$ matters when making connection to gradient penalty and weight decay

> The authors may need to show whether the proposed input perturbation is complementary or replicated with gradient penalty and weight decay, otherwise, this may weaken the contribution of this method.

Thanks for the suggestion of showing the relationship between the training-sampling gap and $\gamma_{t}$.

The connection between input perturbation, weight decay and gradient penalty is that they all are methods of achieving Lipschitz continuity, which is able to reduce the exposure bias. Weight decay and gradient penalty realize Lipschitz continuity by explicitly limiting the model weights, In contrast, input perturbation is an implicit way of achieving Lipschitz continuity. But input perturbation has advantages in both training cost and sample quality compared with the other two methods. 

> As a plug-in method to diffusion model and recently there are various choices in speeding up the sampling, e.g., DDIM, the authors may need to explore if input perturbation can be compatible with these techniques.

We have experimentally shown that input perturbation is compatible with DDIM sampling. Furthermore, our method has a favourable property for speed-up sampling: the fewer sampling step we use, the more FID gain we get from DDIM. Unfortunately, the results came out after the deadline for the paper modification.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper considers the discrepancy between training and inference time of diffusion models, which the authors term "exposure bias". Specifically, diffusion models obtain perturbed training point $x_t$ (at time $t$) by pushing the training data $x_0 \sim p_0$ (at time $0$) through some predefined Gaussian kernel $p_{t0}(\cdot|x_0)=\mathcal{N}(\sqrt{\alpha_t}x_0, 1-\alpha_t)$. During sampling, the distribution of samples at time $t$ is no longer the group-truth $p_{t0}*p_0$ due to the estimation error / discretization error. As a result, there is a training-sampling mismatch. To alleviate this issue, the authors propose to add small amount of noise to the neural network input during training. The noise mimics the estimation error / discretization error during sampling. Experimentally, the proposed method improves the generation quality over the baseline ADM on three image datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strong points

- The studied problem (exposure bias) is crucial for diffusion models, especially when the network architecture has relatively low capacity. 

- The proposed method is straightforward to implement as a regularization. 

- Experimental evidence supports the effectiveness of the proposed method.

### Weak points

- The authors provide little formal reasoning for the source of exposure bias. The exposure bias of diffusion models is actually observed and studied in more detail by previous work [1]. In their Section 5.2, they show that VP (continuous version of Diffusion Models) suffers from such bias due to a strong norm-$t$ correlation, leading to catastrophic failure on a weaker architecture. Specifically, using the notation in current paper and the arguments in [1],  the norm $||x_t|| \approx \sqrt{d}\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha_t}}$ for large $t$ (by CLT), where $d$ is the data dimension. During sampling, diffusion model could break down when the trajectories of backward ODEs/SDEs/ancestral sampling deviate from the norm-$t$ relation to which most training samples pertain. It would be helpful to add the reference or include the discussion for completeness/clarity. 

- (Continuing on the point above) The solution proposed by the authors implicitly assumes that the original sampling process of diffusion models will lead to a larger norm, i.e.  $||x_t|| > \sqrt{d}\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha_t}}$. To see this, by the new Algorithm 4, the training norm is now $||x_t|| \approx \sqrt{d}\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha_t}}(1+\gamma_t)^2$. Could you please verify this in practice? 

- (Continuing on the point above) By the analysis above, we know that in Algorithm 4, $||x_t|| \approx \sqrt{d}\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha_t}}(1+\gamma_t)^2$ \--- there is still a strong norm-$t$ relationship in current version, although there is a slight difference (several points can have the same target $\epsilon$). Does it contradict the arguments in [1]? 

- (Continuing on the point above) Since the proposed method may not really bridge the training-sampling by the point above, the performance gain could be attributed to its regularization effects (other simple regularizers also improve over the baselines). The review thinks it may be helpful to conduct experiments on a weaker architecture (as [1] did) to see which factor contributes the most.

- Adding noise effectively smoothes out the neural output, as suggested by the authors. However, it also deviates from the theoretical foundations of diffusion models. [2] shows that the vanilla denoising objective in diffusion models is indeed estimating the score function. What's the meaning of the new objective in Algorithm 4? This point is important since score functions allow us to run reverse diffusion SDEs or ODEs, which have better performance than the original ancestral sampling of diffusion models.

- How do the authors pick the checkpoint in Table 2, and the hyper-parameters for other regularization methods in Section 7? 


[1] Poisson Flow Generative Models, NeurIPS 2022, https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.11178

[2] Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations, ICLR 2021, https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.13456
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is generally well-written. The idea is novel, but lacking (1) justification/rationale behind it, and (2) theoretical foundations when treating the neural network as score function estimator.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper still lacks (1) justification/rationale behind the proposed method, and (2) theoretical foundations when treating the neural network as score function estimator. In particular, the results seem contradict with an existing work. I lean toward rejection for current version.

content.title: Response to Reviewer g1C9
content.comment:
Dear reviewer, 

Thank you very much for the effort and reviews. We are sorry for our late response due to the stretched GPU resources and heavy experiments.

> The authors provide little formal reasoning for the source of exposure bias. The exposure bias of diffusion models is actually observed and studied in more detail by previous work [1]. In their Section 5.2, they show that VP (continuous version of Diffusion Models) suffers from such bias due to a strong norm- correlation, leading to catastrophic failure on a weaker architecture. Specifically, using the notation in current paper and the arguments in [1],  the norm $\left\| x_t \right\| \approx  \sqrt{d}\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha _{t}}}$
 for large $t$ (by CLT), where $d$ is the data dimension. During sampling, diffusion model could break down when the trajectories of backward ODEs/SDEs/ancestral sampling deviate from the norm- relation to which most training samples pertain. It would be helpful to add the reference or include the discussion for completeness/clarity. 

The input perturbation we used is actually independent of the data perturbation in ordinary DDPM or score-based models (such as [2]). Generally, perturbing data with multiple noise scales (perturb $x_0$ to get $x_t$) corresponds to the Markovian forward diffusion process or the forward SDE in score-based models. By contrast, we further perturb the input $x_t$ to achieve local smoothness.


> (Continuing on the point above) The solution proposed by the authors implicitly assumes that the original sampling process of diffusion models will lead to a larger norm, i.e. $\left\| x_t \right\| > \sqrt{d}\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha _{t}}}$. To see this, by the new Algorithm 4, the training norm is now $\left\| x_t \right\| \approx  \sqrt{d}\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha _{t}}}(1+\gamma _{t})^{2}$. Could you please verify this in practice? 

> (Continuing on the point above) By the analysis above, we know that in Algorithm 4, $\left\| x_t \right\| \approx  \sqrt{d}\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha _{t}}}(1+\gamma _{t})^{2}$ --- there is still a strong norm- relationship in current version, although there is a slight difference (several points can have the same target $\epsilon$). Does it contradict the arguments in [1]? 

Our further experiments on Cifar10 verify the statement above, where we compare the 3 training paradigms:
| **model**     | **input signal**         | **supversion signal**    | **best FID** | **Correlation betwwen $\left\| x_t \right\|$ and $\sqrt{d}\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha _{t}}}$** |
|---------------|--------------------------|--------------------------|--------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| ADM           | $\epsilon$               | $\epsilon$               | 3.56         | 0.57                                                                                    |
| new noise ADM | $\epsilon + \gamma \xi $ | $\epsilon + \gamma \xi $ | 4.09         | 0.61                                                                                    |
| ADM-IP        | $\epsilon + \gamma \xi $ | $\epsilon$               | 3.12         | 0.61                                                                                    |

The new noise ADM and our ADM-IP share the same training norm $\left\| x_t \right\| \approx  \sqrt{d}\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha _{t}}}(1+\gamma _{t})^{2}$, which has a stronger correlation compared with ADM. The new noise ADM is worse than ADM due to its stronger norm-t correlation. So, this is consistent with the argument in [1]. However, the asymmetry between the input signal and supervision signal in our input perturbation leads to a better FID, this is the core of our method.


> (Continuing on the point above) Since the proposed method may not really bridge the training-sampling by the point above, the performance gain could be attributed to its regularization effects (other simple regularizers also improve over the baselines). The review thinks it may be helpful to conduct experiments on a weaker architecture (as [1] did) to see which factor contributes the most.

The reason that we also show the effectiveness of **weight decay** and **gradient penalty** is that achieving **Lipschitz continuity** is a way to alleviate the exposure bias and Lipschitz continuity can be achieved by weight decay, gradient penalty and our input perturbation. But **input perturbation** shows the advantages in both training cost and sample quality compared with the other two methods.

> Adding noise effectively smoothes out the neural output, as suggested by the authors. However, it also deviates from the theoretical foundations of diffusion models. Thanks for the insightful comment. The score function indeed is important to do reverser diffusion and it requires a relatively large gradient in the neural network to gradually run the SDEs/ODEs. In reality, ADM-IP just achieves a slightly smoother prediction function (about 10% reduction of the gradient norm), input perturbation does not worsen the reverse diffusion.

For each model, we select the checkpoint that generates the best FID with 1000 sampling steps.
We select the hyper-parameters for weight decay and gradient penalty by grid search.
